name: Islamic Socialism
summary: Islamic socialism holds that the Qur'an, the hadith and the early caliphate's welfare practice support social justice, curbs on hoarding and usury, and an active state guaranteeing the needs of the poor. It accepts property as a trust conditioned on duty to the community and favours zakat, welfare and nationalisation of key industries, while rejecting Marxist atheism and usually class war. Adherents range from reformist democrats such as the Pakistan Peoples Party to authoritarian regimes such as Siad Barre's Somalia and Gaddafi's Libya.
scope: The mainstream religious-reformist strand: Mustafa al-Siba'i's Syrian 'Socialism of Islam', al-Afghani, Perwez and the Pakistan Peoples Party under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, with Nasser-era Arab socialism and Somalia's SRSP as state examples. Gaddafi's Green Book (wage abolition, equal partnership) is a radical variant used only where marked; Marxist-influenced Iranian groups such as Shariati's are noted but not the basis. Many modern-issue answers are inferred with low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Mustafa al-Siba'i
keyFigures.role: Syrian Muslim Brotherhood leader and author of The Socialism of Islam (1959).

keyFigures.name: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Pakistan Peoples Party, which pursued Islamic socialism and nationalisation.

keyFigures.name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
keyFigures.role: Nineteenth-century reformer credited with early Islamic-socialist ideas.

sources.title: Islamic socialism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Strands, thinkers, positions on property, zakat, riba, welfare, democracy, sharia and nationalisation.

sources.title: Sosialisme Islam Menurut Mustafa al-Siba'i (Islamic Socialism According to Mustafa al-Siba'i)
sources.author: Ismail, Long and Jasni, Rabbanica 5(2), 2024
sources.usedFor: Al-Siba'i's rights (life, liberty, property, dignity, women) and the social solidarity (al-takaful al-ijtimai) doctrine.

sources.title: The Green Book, Part Two: The Solution of the Economic Problem
sources.author: Muammar Gaddafi
sources.usedFor: Radical variant: wage-labour as slavery, equal shares of the factors of production, possession beyond need as exploitation.

sources.title: Pakistan Peoples Party
sources.author: Dawn
sources.usedFor: PPP founding by Bhutto, nationalisation, land reform and labour-rights stance.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Al-Siba'i's duty of social solidarity makes the state and community guarantors of care for the sick and poor, and the Islamic welfare tradition of the bayt al-mal is cited as precedent.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not a theme of the founding texts, but insistence on a just wage and PPP labour-rights policy imply support for a substantial legal floor.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Islamic socialists reject laissez-faire capitalism as exploitative and want the state to secure justice, though they keep markets and private trade within moral limits.

public-ownership.rationale: Bhutto's PPP nationalised banks, insurance and major industries, and Somalia's SRSP nationalised banks and oil distribution, with key industries seen as held for the community.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Zakat is a compulsory levy on accumulated wealth and adherents see hoarding as sinful, so heavier burdens on the rich follow from core doctrine.

unions-good.rationale: PPP-style Islamic socialism claimed to serve workers and peasants and advanced labour rights, though state-led unions were often kept under control.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property is a protected right (al-Siba'i, Afghani) but it is conditional on duties to the needy and ultimately God's, and may be nationalised, so not very hard to override.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Curbing concentrated private wealth and enforcing social duty on business is core, and PPP policy went beyond regulation to nationalisation.

cut-welfare.rationale: Solidarity (al-takaful al-ijtimai) obliges society and state to provide for the poor, orphans, elderly and sick, so cutting welfare contradicts the doctrine.

worker-ownership.rationale: Gaddafi's partners-not-wage-workers slogan favours it, but mainstream Islamic socialists (Siba'i, Bhutto) favoured state ownership and zakat welfare instead.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic socialist regimes were often authoritarian, but al-Siba'i's rights of liberty bar jailing without proven offence, so adherents split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Al-Siba'i's right to life and health, with Islam forbidding harmful intoxicants, makes legal recreational drugs unacceptable to adherents.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed directly; the dignity of all humans regardless of race is stressed, but free expression is also affirmed, and regimes varied.

strong-leader.rationale: Bhutto's slogan joined socialism with democracy and legitimacy comes from the public, though Islamic socialist regimes often had strongmen, so adherents are split.

state-harmful.rationale: The state is the guarantor of social security and zakat, and Islamic socialists want an active state, not its abolition.

limit-guns.rationale: No doctrine on guns; Islamic socialism's concern for life and order points mildly to limits, but nothing is stated.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not a doctrinal matter; the right to life and security is protected, but regimes differed and no position is stated.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Al-Siba'i holds that freedom cannot override sharia limits, and sex work is a prohibited act in Islamic law.

decide-locally.rationale: Adherents favoured a strong central state for nationalisation and redistribution, though Bhutto's PPP later extended provincial autonomy.

rehabilitation.rationale: Al-Siba'i upholds qisas and imprisonment for proven offenders, but welfare and mercy are also stressed, so the question is undetermined.

traditional-family.rationale: Islamic socialists ground society in Islamic family law and ethics, and Gaddafi and al-Siba'i stress women's family roles alongside rights.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Al-Siba'i's study rejects freedom claims that breach sharia and names LGBT claims as examples, and Islamic socialists treat the issue as outside legitimate rights.

abortion-legal.rationale: Al-Siba'i's right to life is protected except by sharia, implying restriction, though the specific issue is not addressed.

more-religion-public.rationale: The premise of the ideology is that Islam should guide economic and social life, and Bhutto's slogan names Islam as the party's faith.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Al-Siba'i insists on the equal dignity of all people and anti-imperial equality, but remedial racial programmes are not discussed.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Gaddafi and al-Siba'i see natural differences between the sexes; the question is not directly addressed.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Islamic socialists combine anti-imperialism with defence of Islamic and national identity against Western ideology.

gradual-change.rationale: Reformers like al-Siba'i and Bhutto acted by legislation and gradual reform, while Gaddafi and Somalia's Barre came by coup; adherents are split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The doctrine is silent on immigration levels, and umma solidarity pulls against restriction.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Anti-imperial and non-aligned in orientation, they distrusted Western-led institutions, though not hostile to cooperation.

free-trade.rationale: Anti-imperialism and nationalisation of trade and industry make adherents sceptical of unrestricted trade, though this is inferred.

nation-first.rationale: Pan-Islamic solidarity and nationalism both pull; Bhutto stressed independent foreign policy, but no stated position on global cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Anti-imperial adherents distrust Western military intervention, inferred from their anti-colonial stance.

open-borders.rationale: Not a stated position; Muslim states are bounded, and the umma ideal does not imply open borders generally.

limit-growth.rationale: Development and welfare for the poor are priorities, and Islamic socialists favoured industrialisation; environmental limits were not discussed.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Modern issue not addressed by the founding authors; no stated stance.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine, which treats justice as primarily moral and religious.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; Bhutto's Pakistan did pursue nuclear capability, but this was security policy rather than doctrine.

revolution-justified.rationale: Gaddafi and Barre took power by coup and Iranian groups used revolution, but al-Siba'i and Bhutto pursued reform through law and elections, so adherents split.

experts-over-public.rationale: Bhutto's slogan puts democracy as the polity, and legitimacy is said to derive from the people, though scholars have a guiding role.

central-planning.rationale: Nationalisation of key industries and state-directed economic reform were the means adopted by PPP Pakistan and Somalia's scientific socialism.

socialized-markets.rationale: Islamic socialists accept trade and private earnings alongside public enterprise, though they do not frame it as market socialism.

land-value-tax.rationale: Not discussed; land is held to belong to God and regulated, but this specific tax is not a doctrine.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Islamic inheritance law spreads estates by fixed shares, and adherents favour curbing concentration, but heavy inheritance tax is not stated.

basic-income.rationale: Islamic socialists point to Abu Bakr's equal stipend and Umar's pensions as models for a guaranteed income that some want renewed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Nationalist industrialisation and anti-imperialism suggest protection, inferred rather than stated.

state-directs-investment.rationale: PPP and SRSP nationalised banks and heavy industry to direct development, and Islamic socialism gave the state the economic lead.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirms the right to own what one earns, and land reform against feudals aimed to spread holdings, but not to the exclusion of public ownership.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Mainstream adherents keep wages and money; only Gaddafi's Green Book calls wage-labour a form of slavery and predicts the end of money and profit.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The state should control banking and credit, and Pakistan nationalised banks, so abolishing central banks is opposed.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Some regimes used state-managed bodies, but doctrine does not call for state-recognised wage and price bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: The PPP claimed democracy, but Somalia's SRSP and Libya's regimes ruled by one party; mainstream adherents oppose a single ideological party.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Anti-feudal reformers were hostile to monarchs, though the early caliphate is idealised; the Gulf monarchies were not allies of the ideology.

democracy-best.rationale: Bhutto's slogan made democracy the party's polity and Islamic socialists say legitimate rule derives from the people, though some regimes were authoritarian.

direct-votes.rationale: Gaddafi's Green Book demands direct democracy via popular congresses, but other adherents accept representative parliaments.

workers-councils.rationale: Mainstream adherents work through parliaments; only Gaddafi's people's committees resemble councils, and he rejects class rule.

right-to-secede.rationale: Nationalist states like Pakistan and Somalia resisted secession, and the umma ideal favours unity; inferred.

natural-rulers.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirms equal dignity of all people and Islam rejects hereditary privilege, though scholars are respected.

political-violence-never.rationale: Adherents accept jihad, war of defence and qisas, and some joined armed movements, so violence is not always unjust.

war-builds-character.rationale: No celebration of war; defence of the community is a duty, but war is not valued as character-forming.

separate-church-state.rationale: The ideology rests on applying Islam to public and economic life, and Wikipedia notes adherents treat socio-economic issues as spiritual matters.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Al-Siba'i grounds law and rights in sharia, but the article notes adherents differ over how far sharia should be implemented.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Defense, justice and security are state duties to the community, and the ideology prefers an active state.

military-superiority.rationale: Not stated; third-world adherents stressed independence and defence, but not dominance over rivals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Al-Siba'i insists there is no superiority of race, language or nation, and the umma is defined by faith.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Most Islamic socialists reject Marxist materialism and class war, preferring solidarity, though some Iranian groups adopted Marxist class analysis.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Zakat and distribution aim to curb extremes, but al-Siba'i affirms differing earnings from effort, so strict equality is not the aim.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not discussed; land belongs to God in the doctrine and no position on Indigenous land arises.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Anti-imperialism is central, so reparations follow naturally, though the sources do not state this.

civilizational-union.rationale: Pan-Islamic solidarity and Muslim unity are common themes, such as Afghani and Sindhi, though regimes were nationalist.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Hoarding is condemned, and duty to neighbours and community, with zakat, is central.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Al-Siba'i couples every individual right with duty and trust, and community guarantee comes first.

limit-population.rationale: Islamic scholars generally reject coercive population control and these thinkers blame unjust distribution rather than numbers.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Islamic socialists wanted development and industrialisation under justice, not rejection of modernity.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Not addressed; they want development, but disrupting institutions is not a stated aim.

human-enhancement.rationale: Sharia limits on bodily alteration and the ideology's moral conservatism suggest scepticism, inferred.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Modern issue; moral and religious accountability of rulers is stressed, so inferred opposition.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: The founding texts predate digital privacy and say nothing on it, so adherents have no stated position.

restore-past-order.rationale: They look to the early caliphate as a model but pursue modern reform and development, so are split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The ideology is explicitly doctrinal and wants policy shaped by Islam and socialism.

direct-action.rationale: The mainstream works through parties, elections and the state, as with the PPP.

means-match-ends.rationale: None of the sources links methods of change to the form of the intended society, and adherents used both reform and coups.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The ideology wants development and a welfare state, not primitivism.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: No source suggests it; they accept differing occupations and earnings from effort.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Al-Siba'i's social solidarity secures needs of the poor and Gaddafi says possession beyond need is exploitation, but earned income is also recognised.

production-for-use.rationale: Wealth is a trust to be used for community welfare and Gaddafi's economics aim at satisfying needs, though profit is not condemned by all.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Afghani opposed improper profit and usury and Gaddafi called profit exploitation, but al-Siba'i recognises lawful earnings, so adherents split.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Islamic socialists generally reject the Marxist atheism and class dictatorship in favour of solidarity and Islamic legitimacy.

collective-farming.rationale: Al-Siba'i protects the right to own what one cultivates, and PPP land reform sought redistribution to peasants rather than collectives.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Anti-imperialism blames Western capitalism for domination, but the war thesis is not stated.

taxation-theft.rationale: Zakat is an obligatory levy on wealth and the state funds welfare, so taxation is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Al-Siba'i says liberty cannot breach sharia, so the state may restrict beyond preventing harm to others.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Al-Siba'i couples individual rights with community guarantee and duties, and the umma has collective claims.

conscription.rationale: Defence of the Islamic community is a duty, but conscription is not specifically discussed.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Bhutto's slogan makes democracy central, so voice outranks exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Government as a guarantor of welfare, not a business competing for customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Al-Siba'i grounds social security in guaranteeing material conditions, and Islamic socialists treat poverty as a denial of real freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: The sources do not discuss the political weight of universities and media, so no position can be inferred.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Al-Siba'i stresses that no race or people is more noble than another.

organic-representation.rationale: Bhutto's PPP competed in parliamentary elections as a party, so party democracy is accepted; Gaddafi, by contrast, rejects parties.

total-state.rationale: They want an active economic state but also protect individual rights and religion, rather than state direction of all life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Anti-colonial renewal themes exist but no radical rebirth doctrine is stated.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Anti-imperial; non-aligned regimes did not advocate expansion, though pan-Islamic unity is favoured.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal bonds are the very thing the PPP's land reform and anti-feudal stance opposed.

bound-labor.rationale: Land reform against feudal landlords and rights of the cultivator reject bonded labour.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Revelation is treated as the standard of truth, but the sources do not take up the claim that knowledge reflects power.

universal-morality.rationale: Al-Siba'i grounds rights in the natural order and revelation common to humanity, so universal truths exist, though known through revelation.

single-common-good.rationale: Islamic socialists posit a single just order from revelation, with social solidarity superseding competing interests.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Anti-imperial, pan-Islamic and Arab adherents oppose Zionism; Salama Moussa and Nasserist-era thinkers saw Israel as imperial, inferred from stance.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is not a theme of Islamic socialist writing, which centres on economic justice and religion.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Gaddafi's partnership model supports it, but others favour state ownership and managers.

school-vouchers.rationale: Al-Siba'i makes education a state duty to eradicate ignorance, so adherents prefer public provision.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Active state welfare and development spending suggest willingness to run deficits, inferred.

economic-freedom.rationale: Islamic socialists reject the claim that economic freedom, meaning capitalism, undergirds liberty.

rule-by-example.rationale: The early caliphs' personal piety, such as Umar's, is held up as the model for rulers.

national-self-determination.rationale: Anti-colonial nationalism is central, as with Moussa's nationalism against British rule and Sukarno.

force-without-un.rationale: Sources are silent on UN authorisation for force; non-aligned adherents distrusted great-power action but nothing is stated.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Faith and revelation are the source of social and economic guidance, and they reject secular materialism.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Zakat is for the poor within the community; doctrine on immigrants is not stated.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Umar's welfare did not tolerate begging and laziness, but the disabled, orphans and sick are cared for unconditionally, so adherents split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Rather than class struggle, they stress mutual help (tawun) and solidarity among all classes under Islam.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The early caliphate and scripture are revered, and they want cultural heritage preserved.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-imperial, non-aligned orientation favoured a common front of the formerly colonised, and Bhutto stressed an independent foreign policy.

workers-nation.rationale: Islamic socialists stress national or umma solidarity, not an international class, though not explicitly addressed.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Gaddafi stresses natural gender roles, but al-Siba'i supports women's education and public work, so the answer is split.

ban-interest.rationale: Afghani opposed usury citing the Qur'an, and riba is prohibited in Islamic law and by Islamic socialist banking nationalisation.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Al-Siba'i says no race is nobler than another, so legal segregation is rejected.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Mainstream adherents see the state as a guarantor of justice, not simply a ruling-class tool, though some Marxist-influenced strands differ.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Oil nationalisation was a goal of SRSP and Libya, and development was prioritised, inferred.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Assimilation of migrants is not discussed; Muslim-world thinkers wrote about the umma, not immigration policy.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy of this kind is not part of the doctrine, and umma solidarity makes it unlikely to be central.

national-mission.rationale: Pan-Islamic mission to spread Islam exists, but not their form of government, and sources do not address it.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Islamic socialists such as al-Siba'i defend Islam against claims that it restricts women while supporting reform in education and work.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The PPP founded itself against Ayub Khan's crony capitalism, and anti-feudal populism targets elites.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Dignity and equal rights of all humans, including the sick and disabled, who are guaranteed community care.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Not addressed; accountability and liberty from arbitrary detention are affirmed, but regimes abused them.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state has welfare, zakat and economic duties well beyond security.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Al-Siba'i says all humans are children of Adam with equal honour regardless of race.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Al-Siba'i's right of dignity holds all people equal regardless of race, religion, language or status.

socialism-one-country.rationale: National roads to socialism within Muslim states were the norm, unlike Marxist internationalism.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Anti-imperial adherents tend to view settler colonialism as colonialism, inferred from stance.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Sharia-based family and civil law for Muslims conflicts with a single code for all religions.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not addressed in sources; apostasy law is debated.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Livestock slaughter is lawful in Islam and part of zakat and sacrifice, so a ban is rejected.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The ideology wants Islam in public life, and al-Siba'i treats religious education as a state duty.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist theory not used in this ideology, which is not addressed.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Legitimacy derives from the public, according to the article, and Bhutto stressed democracy, though some regimes were authoritarian.

trade-surplus.rationale: Export surpluses as a goal are not addressed by the sources, which focus on distribution and nationalisation.

population-transfer.rationale: Al-Siba'i's rights to dignity, property and liberty rule out expulsion of people.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Cooperation (ta'awun) and solidarity are favoured, not struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Not addressed; regimes banned Marxist or rival parties, but doctrine is silent.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Al-Siba'i defines freedom as release from service to any creature but God and from injustice, which fits non-domination.

separated-powers.rationale: Not addressed; Bhutto's party advocated parliamentary democracy, but detail is missing.

vanguard-party.rationale: Marxist-Leninist vanguard ideas were adopted by the PDPA and SRSP, but mainstream adherents rejected them with Marxist atheism.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The core claim is that Qur'an and zakat put the poor first and Al-Siba'i names the poor, orphans and sick as primary beneficiaries.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing and tenant purchase is a British policy debate absent from Islamic socialist writing.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Pro-worker orientation makes restrictions unwelcome, though regimes limited strikes.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Poverty is blamed on unjust distribution and hoarding, not numbers, as Perwez's view of a poor economic order shows.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirms the equality of all peoples and the umma is multi-ethnic.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not part of Islamic political thought, which uses election, consultation or appointment.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Al-Siba'i allows liberty to be restricted for national defence, but regimes' emergency use was criticised; split.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Al-Ghazali's food reserves precedent and PPP's state intervention suggest willingness, but it is inferred.

party-controls-media.rationale: Gaddafi's Green Book wants public ownership of media but not party control; al-Siba'i affirms free expression.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not a feature of mainstream doctrine, which keeps the army under the state.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation periods are not addressed in the sources, so adherents have no stated position.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Rulers' humble example (Umar) is admired, but pay rules are not a doctrine.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Binding party discipline is not discussed; the PPP was a mass party but doctrine says nothing on member obligations.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Pan-Islamic union is favoured by some, but pooling in the EU kind of union is not discussed.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Not addressed; the caliphate model gives the ruler command, but modern adherents were split.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Islam has no bishops; this is out of scope, inferred as negative.

clerical-rule.rationale: Most Islamic socialists sought legitimacy through the public and modern states, and Iran's clerical rule is a different strand.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Defence of the community is a duty and nationalism is central, so working for one's government's defeat is rejected.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Moral conservatism favours it, but al-Siba'i affirms free expression; split and unstated.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Not addressed; adherent leaders like Gaddafi ruled indefinitely, but Bhutto's democratic claim cuts against.

recall-officials.rationale: Not addressed, though accountable rulers are idealised.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Non-aligned, independent foreign policy was a PPP foundation demand.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Gaddafi's Green Book calls renting exploitation, but mainstream adherents do not.

people-in-arms.rationale: Not part of mainstream doctrine; Gaddafi's armed people is a variant.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Not addressed; peasants are championed but urban life is not condemned.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Pan-Islamic and anti-colonial thinkers support undoing colonial borders, inferred.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Not addressed; al-Siba'i, a professor, values education highly.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirms equal dignity of peoples, but Islam is held to be the superior guide, so split.

death-penalty.rationale: Al-Siba'i upholds qisas for intentional killing under sharia, and Islamic law punishes grave crimes.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Sharia-bound conservative morality makes gender-equality curricula contested, though education is stressed, inferred.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Religious believers might favour it, but the sources do not discuss evolution teaching, so no stance is stated.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Moral limits under sharia and al-Siba'i's view that freedom cannot breach shariah support restriction.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules are not covered in the sources, which stress the umma and equal dignity but not descent versus birth.

minority-language-support.rationale: Minority language policy is not addressed in the sources on this ideology.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Not addressed; sharia for Muslims favours religious law but exemptions are unaddressed.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Collective virtue and the community's moral order are valued over eccentricity, inferred.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Anti-imperialism and the riba ban favour cancellation of poor countries' debts, but it is inferred.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Bhutto's nationalisations and the socialism of anti-colonial leaders presumed political independence needs economic transformation.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Sources do not address how constitutions should be drafted, though Bhutto's party sought elected parliamentary government.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Authoritarian regimes did so, but the doctrine claims democracy, so split.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Zakat and solidarity of the umma imply duties of the wealthy to the poor, though global aid is not stated.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Pakistan pursued it under Bhutto, but it is security policy, not doctrine.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The method of choosing a head of state is not addressed by al-Siba'i or the PPP sources used here.

central-bank-independence.rationale: They want public control of banking and credit for social goals, and oppose interest as such.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property is held in trust, with duties to the needy, and Afghani retained rights subject to providing for those in need.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Not addressed; they were wary of Soviet atheism, but al-Siba'i called for cooperation with the USSR.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk policy is a modern issue the founding sources do not discuss.

collective-defense.rationale: Muslim solidarity favours mutual defence among allies, inferred.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: They want Islam in public life, but Siba'i and Bhutto would not subordinate clergy; Gaddafi sidelined ulama, so low.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not address ceremonial or nonpartisan heads of state; adherent regimes had executive presidents or strongmen.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Pakistan and Somalia fought separatists, but doctrine is silent.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special autonomy arrangements within a larger state are not addressed by the sources.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Islam has no divine descent for rulers, and the ideology cites the humble early caliphs.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Wealth levies like zakat and progressive redistribution are central.

character-from-environment.rationale: Perwez described hell as a society under an evil socio-economic system, treating circumstances as shaping people.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rulers are bound by sharia and accountable to the public.

space-expansion.rationale: Space exploration is not addressed by the sources and is not tied to the doctrine of social justice.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-government theory is not part of Islamic socialist writing, so no stance is stated.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Al-Siba'i accepts qisas, jihad of defence and state coercion for justice, so a rule against ever initiating force is not his; the exact principle is not discussed.

leader-cult.rationale: Reformist Islamic socialists ground legitimacy in Qur'anic justice rather than devotion to a person; the cults around Gaddafi and Siad Barre belong to the authoritarian variant, so this is inferred.

equal-parenting.rationale: Inferred from the classical sharia custody rules these thinkers keep, which favour the mother for young children, while al-Siba'i's rights for women do not extend to an equal-time presumption.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Islamic socialists reject Marxist class war and atheism, favouring solidarity and a state that guarantees needs.

land-redistribution.rationale: The PPP and other Islamic socialist programmes stressed land reform against feudal landlords.

refugee-return.rationale: Solidarity with Palestinians is common in Arab and Islamic socialist regimes; inferred.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Regimes such as Somalia's pursued ethnic irredentism while reformists did not; adherents split.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Reformists such as al-Siba'i stress rights and were mixed on compulsion, while authoritarian variants differed; split.

women-must-cover.rationale: Reformist Islamic socialists such as the PPP did not demand compulsory covering; inferred.

common-currency.rationale: They stress national economic control and nationalisation, which weighs against giving up a national currency; inferred.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Nasser-era Arab socialism and Gaddafi pursued pan-Arab unity; the reformist strand is less explicit.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents have no settled view.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred as no settled view.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: They reject Marxist materialism and ground social justice in the Qur'an and religious ethics.

ban-cartels.rationale: Curbs on hoarding and concentrated wealth fit antitrust action; inferred.

no-bailouts.rationale: An active state that nationalises key industries would rescue them rather than let them fail; inferred.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Reformist democrats and authoritarian regimes within the family disagree, and sharia also limits majorities; split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirmed women's rights, but quotas are not addressed in the sources; split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Nationalisation and anti-imperial stances favour national economic control; inferred.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: The PPP's labour-rights stance suggests support for labour standards in trade; inferred.

moral-incentives.rationale: Al-Siba'i's duty of social solidarity and Gaddafi's equal-partnership model replace pay incentives with community duty.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The reformist mainstream, such as the PPP, worked through politics and the state, though Gaddafi-style regimes came to power by coup; inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The PPP's campaign against feudal landlords suggests opposition to inherited privilege; inferred.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Inferred: Islamic socialists stress Islamic identity and heritage against Western influence, so teaching history from an Islamic standpoint fits, though no text addresses it.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Inferred: Islamic socialists were anti-colonial, and Nasser-era and Bhutto-era movements condemned imperial rule, so tutelage by advanced societies is rejected.

patriotic-education.rationale: Inferred: state-led Islamic socialist regimes promoted national and Islamic loyalty in schools, though nation and flag are secondary to the community.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Inferred: Islamic socialists stress social justice for the poor over race, but the policy was never addressed in their texts.

public-money-creation.rationale: Islamic socialists oppose usury and favour nationalising key industries, which supports public control of money, though no explicit program is stated.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Islamic socialists share the socialist view that capitalism produces injustice and hoarding, and that Islamic social justice should replace it, though they do not hold a collapse theory like Marx's.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Inferred: Arab socialism and Bhutto's party opposed imperial legacies and sought non-aligned independence, so cultivating influence in former imperial lands is disfavoured.

delink-world-market.rationale: Inferred: Islamic socialist regimes such as Gaddafi's Libya and Siad Barre's Somalia pursued nationalisation and independence from Western markets, though not all favoured full delinking.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Inferred: the thesis is a Marxist one, which Islamic socialists reject in its class form, though they denounce imperial exploitation, so adherents are split.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Islamic socialists hold that property is a trust conditioned on duty to the community and favour guaranteed rights for all, so unrestricted discrimination is rejected.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Inferred: al-Siba'i affirms individual rights, but state-led regimes such as Gaddafi's and Siad Barre's did not accept entrenched limits on government, so adherents are split.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Arab and Pakistani socialists defined themselves against colonialism; inferred, with no treaty doctrine stated.

elective-rulers.rationale: The PPP and reformist strands favour elected government, though Gaddafi and Barre ruled without elections.

minority-veto.rationale: Inferred from the collective emphasis on social solidarity over individual claims.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Inferred from Islamic reformist tradition that unjust rulers lose legitimacy.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Inferred from the PPP's parliamentary politics, tempered by the primacy of sharia.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Inferred from the Islamic ethic of kindness to animals.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred from Islamic law allowing animal use under rules requiring mercy.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Al-Siba'i's social solidarity and zakat make care for the poor a binding duty of the rich, with property held as a trust.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Islamic socialism calls for an active state and community responsible for social justice, so withdrawal is rejected.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Inferred from the socialist critique of media serving elites, with no specific source.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Inferred from the socialist view that elites rule through institutions as well as force, with no specific source.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Arab socialism and Gaddafi's Green Book denounce foreign exploitation of poor countries' resources.

native-born-offices.rationale: Inferred from Islamic universalism and al-Siba'i's equal rights; no position stated.

party-own-road.rationale: Islamic socialism presents its own path distinct from Marxism and Soviet direction, as non-aligned Arab socialism did.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Inferred from nationalisation and national-development programmes of Nasser, Bhutto and Barre.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Inferred from the strong Arab and Pakistani nationalist stance on Palestine and Kashmir.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Inferred from anti-colonial stance favouring native rule over settlers.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Not addressed; adherents range from secular-leaning socialists to sharia-first reformers.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Inferred: the socialist and anti-imperial left rejects the equivalence framing.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Not addressed; inferred acceptance of the mainstream historical view.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Inferred from the anti-colonial left's hostility to colonial-era commemoration.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; al-Siba'i's rights doctrine gives no stance on this.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Inferred from the welfare-oriented protection of the vulnerable; no explicit position.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Islamic socialism presents a 'socialism of Islam' rooted in Muslim sources instead of imported Western or Soviet models.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Split: Somalia, Libya and Nasser's Egypt were military regimes, while the PPP is a civilian party.

paid-care-work.rationale: Inferred from state welfare and social-solidarity commitments; not stated.

filial-duty.rationale: Inferred from the Qur'anic duty to parents, which Islamic socialists treat as part of the social solidarity they ground in Islam.

office-by-exam.rationale: Inferred: the strand has no stated civil-service doctrine, and Arab socialist and PPP regimes mixed technocratic and political appointments.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Nationalisation of key industries and state control of the economy imply keeping strategic firms out of foreign hands.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Inferred: the strand upholds Islamic family law and treats the family as a social trust.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Reformist PPP democrats and Gaddafi's popular-committee system differ, so no shared answer.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The state is the guarantor of the poor's needs, and private market schemes run against its stress on solidarity and zakat.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Property is a trust conditioned on duty to the community; the Green Book variant states land belongs to no one and only users may hold it.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred from the PPP's parliamentary-democratic form, though authoritarian variants like Gaddafi's Libya rejected parliaments.

single-official-language.rationale: No source addresses language policy, and adherents range from Arab nationalist to Pakistani and Somali settings.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Inferred from the nationalisation and anti-imperialist stance of the strand.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Inferred: the strand stresses economic justice but has no stated view on race-based legal tests.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Its curbs on hoarding and its ethic of moderation and social duty count against pursuit of ever more possessions.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Split: Gaddafi's Libya armed insurgents abroad while reformist strands such as the PPP did not.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Inferred from the anti-imperialist and anti-hegemonic stance of the strand.

corporate-influence.rationale: Adherents oppose capitalist concentration of wealth and favour nationalising key industries, as the PPP did.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Inferred from anti-imperialism of Nasser-era and PPP socialism.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Inferred from the stress on family and community in al-Siba'i's social solidarity; no program is stated.

residents-only-property.rationale: Inferred from land reform and property held as a trust conditioned on duty to the community.

job-guarantee.rationale: Social solidarity makes the state and community guarantors of the needs of the poor, and the PPP backed labour rights.

democratic-peace.rationale: Not addressed by the founding texts; adherents split between democratic and authoritarian regimes.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Inferred: obedience is owed to a just government acting for social justice, not to law as such.

non-intervention.rationale: Inferred from anti-imperialism and non-alignment in Nasser-era Arab socialism and Bhutto's PPP.

industrial-unions.rationale: Inferred: socialist labour policy favours large national unions, but no texts address union structure.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Inferred: nothing in the sources attributes a minority conspiracy; the focus is social justice.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Inferred from al-Siba'i's defence of the family and rights of women within Islamic law.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Inferred from the democratic reformist strand such as the PPP, which stresses accountability to the people.

local-production.rationale: Inferred from nationalisation and self-reliance of the state examples, which favoured domestic production.

informal-organisation.rationale: Inferred: the state examples and the PPP were centralised, organised parties and the strand favours a strong state.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Inferred: state-led socialist programs asserted national sovereignty over foreign legal constraints.

religious-nation.rationale: Adherents ground economics in Islam, though the strand ranges from secular-leaning PPP to religious reformists.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred: Nasser-era and Bhutto-era Islamic socialists were anti-imperial and non-aligned, rejecting tribute or submission to a power.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Pooling and redistribution according to need is core to al-Siba'i's social solidarity, and PPP and Arab socialist states redistributed across regions.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Islamic socialists accept personal property as a trust while placing key industries and land under public control; Gaddafi's variant also guards personal needs.

defeat-communism.rationale: They reject communism as atheist and materialist, as recorded in this audit's own missing statement, though they favoured non-alignment and not war on it.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Inferred: state provision and nationalisation are preferred for essential services, though private and waqf charity are accepted as supplements.

religion-illusion.rationale: Islamic socialists reject Marxist atheism and treat religion as the source of social justice, not a consolation that fades.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: They condemn capitalism for usury and hoarding and see it as exploitative, not as a stage building a better society.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Inferred: al-Siba'i affirms women's rights within Islamic norms, and states stressed economic participation, but no source ties equality to transforming the economy.

socialized-care.rationale: Inferred: their welfare focus is on the poor and sick, while they uphold the family under Islamic norms, so public kitchens and nurseries are not endorsed.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred: no stated language policy; Arabic is revered but purging loanwords is not a theme of the strand.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred: Islamic ethics honour covenants, but these regimes were centralising and no position on internal treaties is documented.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Inferred: they favour cooperatives and state-led ownership, but not small self-governing communes holding property in common; Gaddafi's partnership model is the nearest, marked variant.

majority-settlement.rationale: Inferred: no stated position; some regimes settled majority groups in minority regions, but it is not part of the doctrine.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Islamic socialism presents itself as a distinct Islamic third way, rejecting both Marxist communism and capitalism.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Islamic socialism has no stated doctrine on land claims and its advocates range from Pakistan to Libya; inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The doctrine's social-justice basis gives no support to Holocaust denial; inferred.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Reformists and regimes differ on sharia penalties; adherents are split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Adherents range from democratic reformists such as the PPP to authoritarian regimes such as Siad Barre's Somalia, so they are split.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Adherents are split between religious-law regimes and secular reformists; no stated position.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Nasser-era Arab socialism and Bhutto's PPP were anti-colonial and opposed exploitation of dependent territories.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Adherents generally accept resistance to invasion of Muslim lands as a religious duty; inferred from the religious grounding.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Reformist democrats such as the PPP use ballots rather than forcible removal over religious law; inferred.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Gaddafi's Green Book calls for direct popular rule and the PPP stressed power for ordinary people; the strands differ.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Islamic socialism treats class injustice as central but has no stated doctrine on race and gender overlap.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Al-Siba'i's rights doctrine rests on Qur'anic family norms, which gives no support for gender identity recognition; inferred.

assisted-dying.rationale: Its religious grounding opposes assisted dying; inferred.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: It joins socialist economics with religious values, which fits combining ideas of left and right; inferred.

alienated-labor.rationale: Al-Siba'i and Gaddafi's Green Book criticise wage labour and hoarding as exploiting workers.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Islamic socialists present Islam as a source of reform, not as a clash with the West; inferred.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Adherents ground their economics in the Qur'an and hadith, which treats God as the source of norms; the PPP was more secular.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: No stated position, and adherents range from secular PPP to religious regimes.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: The PPP took a pro-labour stance, so limiting the means employers use to bury harassment complaints fits; inferred.

social-market-economy.rationale: Property is a trust conditioned on duty, with markets alongside zakat, welfare and nationalised key industries, a mixed economy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Regimes such as Nasser's, Siad Barre's and Gaddafi's built armies, but doctrine does not discuss abolition; inferred.

rich-first.rationale: The doctrine's curbs on hoarding and its call for equal shares oppose letting some grow rich first.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Nasser-era and other Islamic-socialist states favoured non-alignment; inferred.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Islamic socialist states were mostly republics (Nasser, Bhutto, Barre, Gaddafi) and stress social justice over lineage, though some leaders groomed heirs; inferred.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Islamic socialists cite the ban on riba (usury) and want credit that serves the community, which fits cost-based mutual credit though the state often runs banks instead.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Bhutto's PPP and other Islamic socialists were nationalist and anti-imperialist, so refusing outside lender conditions fits, though no source states it; inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: Al-Siba'i grounds equal rights and social solidarity for all, and the PPP stood for broad labor and land reform, so limiting the vote to the propertied is rejected.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Al-Siba'i's rights doctrine covers women within an Islamic frame but does not link their position to nature; the ecological claim is not part of the doctrine, so this is inferred.

reification.rationale: Gaddafi's Green Book calls wage labor a form of slavery and condemns the economic forces that rule workers, which loosely fits the claim; Islamic socialists in general are critical of capitalism.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: As critics of wealth concentration, Islamic socialists would see the rich as dominating the means of speech, though none state it; inferred.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Islamic socialists hold that sharia, a fixed body of law, binds rulers, though several regimes governed by decree; inferred from the reformist strand.

racial-franchise.rationale: Al-Siba'i's doctrine rests on equal rights for all and Islamic socialists reject nationalism by blood; no source supports a racial franchise.

online-participation.rationale: Islamic socialists favor broad popular participation (the PPP was a mass party and the Green Book urges direct popular rule), so online participation fits though it is anachronistic; inferred.

open-government-data.rationale: Reformist Islamic socialists stress accountability of rulers to the community, so open records fit; no source discusses it directly.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Islamic socialists accept sharia family law, which restricts Muslim women from marrying non-Muslims, though their focus is economic; inferred.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Al-Siba'i's social solidarity and equal dignity cover all people, so shunning a minority's businesses is out of keeping with the doctrine; inferred.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Adherents range from democratic parties to authoritarian regimes, and none are documented as backing sortition, so the issue is split (inferred).

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Islamic socialism rereads the Qur'an and early caliphate practice as supporting socialism, a modernist reinterpretation at its core, though Gaddafi's variant goes furthest.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Islamic socialists condemn hoarding and concentrated wealth and use zakat and public ownership to spread it, so concentration is seen as corrupting society.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred from traditional Islamic sexual ethics, which the strand does not revise; the issue is outside its economic focus.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The strand rejects Marxist atheism and grounds its programme in the Qur'an, so state promotion of atheism is the opposite of its aims.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: a state-led socialism with a strong state under Nasser, Bhutto and Gaddafi has no tradition of abolishing police or prisons.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Not addressed; inferred as split between majoritarian populist parties like the PPP and consultative (shura) traditions.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Zakat is a compulsory institution run for the poor and the strand wants the state to secure welfare, though it values charity too.

term-limits.rationale: Not addressed; adherents ran leader-centred parties and states, and no position is inferable.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred from a preference for consultation (shura) and party or state leadership over revocable individual delegation.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Not addressed by a strand focused on poverty and social justice; no position inferable.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred from traditional jurisprudence that the strand mostly keeps, though modernist reformists dissent.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred: reformists stress women's rights to property and education, but most keep the traditional view of the husband as head of the household.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Citizenship-based political rights are the norm in Bhutto, Nasser and Gaddafi-era states and the sources never discuss foreign residents; inferred.

rent-control.rationale: Islamic socialism favours state action against hoarding and exploitation, which fits capping rents in shortage, though no source states it; inferred.

abolish-ip.rationale: Property is a trust bound by duty to the community, but the sources do not call for abolishing patents and copyrights; inferred.

uniformed-youth.rationale: State examples such as Nasser's Egypt and Gaddafi's Libya ran mass youth organisations while the reformist strand did not; split and inferred.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Strands differ, as Gaddafi's regime opposed foreign weapons while Bhutto's party pursued a national bomb; inferred.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Arab and Islamic socialist regimes were anti-imperialist and non-aligned, and the Green Book rejects foreign domination; inferred.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Not an issue the sources address and adherents' positions vary by state; inferred.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Al-Siba'i bans usury and hoarding, and the Green Book says wealth should reflect labour, with rewards for useful work rather than rents or interest.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Islamic law allows lethal self-defence and the movement is not pacifist; inferred from that law, as the sources do not discuss it.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The sources stress the umma and early caliphate, with Arab and Pakistani nationalism varying by state; inferred.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Reformist Muslims keep the binary sex taught in scripture and reject the claim that sex is constructed; inferred.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Women are treated as a group with shared rights and duties in Islamic socialist writing rather than a contested category; inferred.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: State examples honour martyrs of the nation and revolution, such as in Nasser-era and Bhutto-era commemoration; inferred.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Social justice is framed as religious duty, but adherents range from reformist democrats to Gaddafi, so no cosmic-struggle claim is shared; inferred.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; adherents have no common view of a homeland's role; inferred.

culture-before-state.rationale: Social reform and state action are treated as parallel, and states such as Nasser's and Barre's built states first; split and inferred.

god-not-male.rationale: Traditional scriptural language for God is retained by Islamic socialists; inferred.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Reformists reinterpret texts toward social justice but treat the Qur'an as authoritative, not subject to a feminist test; inferred.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Socialist egalitarianism and nationalisation of minority-owned firms pull in different ways, and the sources do not settle it; split and inferred.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Not part of the programme; regions are left to the state, and no source proposes merging them by people; inferred.

independent-unions.rationale: Adherents are split: the strand backs unions but Nasser-era and Bhutto-era states kept them under party control.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Islamic socialists reject Marxist class war and atheism, so they do not make working-class rule a test of socialism.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Their state-led welfare and nationalisation of key industries puts essential services in public hands.

second-chamber.rationale: The Pakistan Peoples Party governed under a bicameral constitution; no doctrine on the question, so inferred from this practice.

municipal-property.rationale: They favour nationalisation by the state, not ownership by local communities; Gaddafi's Green Book favours partnership at the workplace instead.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The strand favours a strong national state directing the economy, not confederations of local assemblies; inferred.

family-wage.rationale: They hold that Islam requires the family's needs to be met and favour welfare; inferred from traditional-family and welfare positions.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: The strand does not address drug approval; adherents are split or indifferent.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: The strand does not address ageing research; adherents are split or indifferent.

anonymous-payments.rationale: A state-directed economy with strong oversight favours traceable payments; inferred from their state-led economics.

online-anonymity.rationale: Their regimes controlled speech and organising, so anonymous participation has little support; inferred.

person-over-state.rationale: Property is held as a trust conditioned on duty to the community, but the strand also guards individuals' welfare; adherents are split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: They ground socialism in the Qur'an and hadith and reject materialist Marxism, so politics must serve spiritual as well as material needs.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: They favour a strong national state, so regional powers would sit on the national legislature's authority; inferred.

gm-crops.rationale: The strand does not address genetic engineering; adherents are split or indifferent.

dense-cities.rationale: The strand does not address urban form; adherents are split or indifferent.

racial-group-interests.rationale: They reject class and sectarian division and ground solidarity in faith and social justice; Arab socialist states had a nationalist strain, so not -2.

racial-pride.rationale: Pride defined by race conflicts with the Islamic emphasis on equality of believers; inferred.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Bhutto-era and Nasser-era states stressed defence and non-alignment; inferred since doctrine does not address it.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Islamic socialists ground community in faith and the ummah, though Nasser-era Arab socialism embraced Arab nationhood, so the view is split; inferred.

communal-electorates.rationale: Pakistan's separate electorates were a live issue for adherents, but the strand has no unified position and the sources do not address it.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Anti-imperialism is common among Arab and Pakistani socialist regimes, which framed foreign powers as threats; inferred, not sourced.

free-public-college.rationale: The strand holds that the state should guarantee the needs of the poor through welfare and social solidarity, which supports tuition-free education.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Anachronistic question; Islamic socialism has no stated environmental tax doctrine and favours state action over pricing mechanisms.

future-generations.rationale: Inferred from the Islamic view of property as a trust held for the community; the sources do not discuss future generations.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Al-Siba'i affirmed women's rights within Islamic law, but the strand has no stated view on women's distinct public values.

arms-reduction.rationale: State examples were militarised while reformists favoured peace; adherents split and sources do not settle it.

open-diplomacy.rationale: No stated doctrine; regimes such as Libya and Somalia practised secret diplomacy, while reformist parties spoke of openness.

capital-controls.rationale: Nationalisation of key industries and state direction of the economy, as under Bhutto and Nasser, imply state control over capital movement.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Islamic socialists favour a strong state, so a state monopoly on force follows from their model, though they did not discuss it; inferred.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The tradition accepts jihad and defence of the community and its state examples were militarist, so refusal of orders is inferred as disfavoured.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Al-Siba'i's duty of social solidarity and the PPP's labour programme back workers' organisations and fair wages, though Gaddafi's variant abolished wage labour.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Islamic socialists want the state to guarantee the needs of the poor, so income top-ups fit, though tax credits themselves are not discussed; inferred.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: The tradition favours an active state and nationalisation, which clashes with binding limits on borrowing; inferred.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Islamic socialism arose as anti-imperial thought, and Nasser-era and Bhutto-era regimes pressed for a fairer international economic order.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Reformist adherents want to use the existing state for social justice, while only Gaddafi's variant broke with it; inferred.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The tradition draws a blueprint from the Qur'an and hadith for property and welfare, so open experimentation is not its stance; inferred.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic socialists treat resources as a trust held for the community, which does not suit pricing nature as capital.

sacred-nation.rationale: Nasser-era Arab socialism and Siad Barre's regime were nationalist while al-Siba'i grounded loyalty in faith, so adherents are split.

student-debt-relief.rationale: The movement's state-led welfare orientation favours relief for the indebted, though student loans were not at issue; inferred.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Egalitarian regional redistribution suits the movement's concern for the poor, though it never used this framing; inferred.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Islamic socialists ground social justice in the Qur'an and hadith and in a fixed human nature that carries dignity and duties.

public-service-media.rationale: Regimes of this tradition ran state media, while reformists like the PPP favoured some press freedom; split.

missingStatements.text: Wealth should be taxed by a compulsory annual levy to fund the poor.
missingStatements.rationale: Zakat, about 2.5 percent of accumulated wealth, is the central economic institution of Islamic socialism, which uses it to discourage hoarding.

missingStatements.text: Economic policy should be guided by religious teaching on wealth and charity.
missingStatements.rationale: Adherents ground their economics in the Qur'an and hadith and treat socio-economic questions as spiritual ones.

missingStatements.text: Communism should be rejected because it is atheist and materialist.
missingStatements.rationale: Islamic socialists reject Marxist atheism and materialism while keeping social justice; Bhutto said his programme stood for socialism, not communism.
missingStatements.declined: Rejection of atheist communism is captured by more-religion-public, class-struggle-history and reason-over-faith answers; a separate anti-communism statement would be redundant.

notes: Gaddafi's Green Book and Marxist-influenced Iranian groups would answer differently on wage labour, class struggle and ownership. Sharia implementation is a point of disagreement among thinkers.
